transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, D.C., I'm Dale Willman.
Russia is using familiar tactics in its efforts to influence American voters in the final
stretch to Election Day.
And as NPR's Shannon Bond reports, researchers and U.S. lawmakers say Kremlin-backed influence
operations are ramping up activity.
Russian-backed groups are pumping out fabricated claims about Democratic candidates, AI-manipulated
videos of celebrities, and fake posts imitating real news outlets.
The goal is to exacerbate divisions, erode confidence in democracy, and, crucially, undermine
support for Ukraine.
Darren Linville tracks foreign propaganda campaigns at Clemson University's media forensics
hub.
At the end of the day, the main issue for Russia is and has to be Ukraine.
Researchers say the same Russian operations now active in the U.S. midterms have also
targeted elections this year in France and Germany.
Shannon Bond, NPR News.
Military officials in Ukraine say the Starlink technology that's critical to its war effort
against Russia is still not working properly.
Drone operators say their weapons have been falling out of the sky after a diplomatic
fight between President Trump and Ukraine's leader Volodymyr Zelensky.
Alex Ward is the national security reporter for "The Wall Street Journal."
Well, if you talk to the president, he'll say he's just doing what he can to end the
war and do what's best for the U.S.
And he's, when he talks about the sanctions waiver, he says that had to do with the return
of the imprisoned American, Stephen Hubbard.
Now Hubbard's home, is the president going to impose sanctions to get Russia to the table?
That's unclear.
There's also some people we've been speaking to who say, look, the president is desperate
to end this war, and the one place he has more influence is over Ukraine, not Russia.
So if he can sort of get Ukraine to capitulate into a place that Russia could accept, then
maybe this ends sooner rather than later.
That's "The Wall Street Journal's" Alex Ward.
As President Trump campaigns to keep Republicans in control of Congress, polls show low approval
ratings for the Iran war and high fuel prices.
As NPR's Jill Rose reports, jet fuel climbed to a new record high this week, pushing holiday
airfares to some of their highest levels in years.
The average price for a gallon of jet fuel in the U.S. was $4.90 on Thursday, according
to the tracking firm Argus.
That's the highest single-day average the firm has ever recorded, and more than twice
what the average price was a year ago.
Fuel is one of airlines' biggest expenses, and they are paying billions of dollars more
for it than they did last year.
Carriers are absorbing some of those higher costs, according to the trade group Airlines
for America.
But they're also passing some of those costs on in the form of higher fares.
Fires for Thanksgiving are up about 30 percent compared to last year, while ticket prices
for the Christmas holiday are up more than 20 percent.
Jill Rose, NPR News, Washington.
Stocks fell down across the board on Friday, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average down
652 points.
The NASDAQ closed down by 53 points.
You're listening to NPR News.
Rescuers are continuing to search for survivors in a remote Chinese region in Tibet after
a magnitude-7 earthquake hit the area on Thursday.
At least 16 people are dead and 76 others injured.
The quake collapsed.
Hundreds of homes and officials are worried about more damage from aftershocks, as well
as possible casualties from landslides.
The Pentagon has released a new set of UFO files, NPR's Jeff Brumfield reports.
In June, two FBI agents at an undisclosed facility spotted a black triangular object
several miles to the west of an observation post they were manning.
It rose up over a ridgeline, hovered for several seconds, and then shot into a nearby canyon
at the speed of a fighter jet before disappearing into the shadows.
The report says the unidentified craft was silent and thermal imagery didn't show any
signs of engine exhaust.
In recent years, the government has become increasingly concerned about sighting some
possible Chinese drones around U.S. bases and research sites.
The origin of this specific object remains unknown, but the truth is out there.
Jeff Brumfield, NPR News.
President Trump says he's ordered the administration to file a lawsuit to block certification of
the Senate race in Alaska if the current Republican senator loses.
The suit was filed on Thursday.
Senator Dan Sullivan is being challenged by Democrat Mary Peltola and a third candidate,
also named Dan Sullivan.
Alaska's Supreme Court has previously rejected efforts to remove the other Sullivan from
the ballot.
The Milwaukee Brewers beat Tampa Bay 3-2 Friday night in the first Game of the World series,
Game 2 takes place Saturday in Milwaukee.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.

Ukrainian drone operators report Starlink failures amid tensions between Trump and Zelensky
Jet fuel hits record high, pushing holiday airfares to some of their highest levels in years
Stocks fall broadly Friday, with the Dow down 652 points
Rescuers search for survivors after magnitude-7 earthquake in remote Tibet region kills 16
Pentagon releases new UFO files, including FBI agents' account of a silent triangular object
